verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, on the sheminith. A psalm, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung upon the eighth. A psalm of David.
verses.directors_commentary: Nothing here is plot, but everything here is stage direction. The performer is handed over to a choirmaster, so this was no private lament muttered in a cave: it was a text prepared for the Temple musicians. 'The sheminith' is literally 'the eighth' with the article, as though the singers knew exactly which instrument or tune was meant; we no longer do. Rashi and the Targum say an eight-stringed lyre, Ibn Ezra only a melody. The KJV 'upon Sheminith' simply transliterates, and honestly so; do not let an actor pretend to know more. The Hebrew counts this line as verse 1, which is why every verse number in this psalm runs one higher than the KJV.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'the eighth' (feminine, with the article). Its musical sense is lost: an eight-stringed lyre, an octave or a mode are the proposals. The same term stands over Psalm 6, and the packet's commentators send the reader back to the earlier occurrence.

verses.translation_literal: Save, YHWH, for the faithful one has come to an end, for the trustworthy have vanished from the sons of Adam.
verses.translation_dramatic: Save us, LORD. Look, and see that the faithful one is gone, that those who kept their word have melted from among the children of men.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm begins with a bare imperative, hoshi'ah, a single cry of two syllables before the name of God, and the speaker says why in two matching 'for' clauses. Play it as shock, not sermon: he has looked around and found nobody. Note the singular 'the faithful one' (chasid) beside the plural 'the trustworthy' (emunim): first the loyal friend of God is finished, then the whole fabric of promise-keeping between people. Rashi hears David hunted by Saul, betrayed by those who told Saul where he hid; Radak hears a wicked generation preying on the weak. The KJV 'Help, Lord' is gentler than 'Save', which is the verb of rescue from death; the KJV 'ceaseth' and 'fail' are archaic and make a slow decline, where the Hebrew perfects say 'it is finished, they have vanished'. The 'sons of Adam' is plain humanity, 'the children of men' in the KJV; the Hebrew has the earth-creature in it.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of the verb 'to save, to bring into open space'. It is the cry made to a king for rescue (2 Sam 14:4) and it gives the word 'yesha' of verse 6.
'Has come to an end, is finished'. Rashi glosses it with 'ended'; Meiri takes it as 'a lone one', all the faithful are lost; Ibn Ezra notes that the verb is intransitive.
A word found only here in the Bible. Rashi says it is the same as 'ended' (a root with 'afes) and follows Menachem; the sense 'vanish' is secure, the exact root is not.

verses.translation_literal: Falsehood they speak, each one with his neighbor, a lip of smooth things; with a heart and a heart they speak.
verses.translation_dramatic: Emptiness, nothing but emptiness, passes between neighbor and neighbor: the glossy phrase, the polished lip, and under it a heart and another heart, speaking.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the verse where the speakers become unbearable, so keep them charming. Everything is said with a smile. 'Falsehood' (shav') is more than lying: it is emptiness, a word with nothing in it. 'A lip of smooth things' is the key image; chalaqot comes from the root for 'smooth', a surface with no grip, and it is the word used elsewhere for slippery ground and for flattery. KJV 'flattering lips' gets the sense but loses the touch, the feel of an oiled surface. Then the idiom of the verse: 'with a heart and a heart', literally two hearts, each speaker holding one for the face and one for the knife. The KJV 'a double heart' is fair, but a modern ear takes it for a 'double-minded' dithering, when the Hebrew means a duplicity that is quite deliberate. Rashi hears friendship shown to David and hatred hidden. Ibn Ezra's picture is hard to beat: the tongue pleads for one heart while the other stays silent.

philological_notes.note: 'A lip of smooth things'. A singular 'lip' (here also 'language' as in Gen 11:1) with a plural of smoothness; Ibn Ezra and Radak say a noun is missing, 'smooth words'.
Literally 'with a heart and a heart', two hearts, a repeated noun for duplicity (compare 1 Chr 12:34). Rashi: they show peace to me, hatred is hidden in their hearts.

verses.translation_literal: May he cut off, YHWH, all lips of smoothnesses, a tongue speaking great things.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the LORD cut them away: every lip polished smooth, every tongue that swells with big talk. Let him cut them off, root and branch.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalmist stops lamenting and prays, in a single hard verb. Karat is the verb used for cutting, that is, making, a covenant (karat berit): the ancient treaty was sealed by cutting, and a broken one was answered by cutting the oath-breaker. It also means cutting a person off from his people, the penalty in the law for the gravest offences. So the word carries both senses at once: a tongue that swore smooth words is cut off the way a covenant is cut. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri differ only on whether this is prayer or prophecy; the Hebrew form can be either, and the actor should keep both in the voice, a wish that is also a verdict.

The KJV 'flattering lips' tames the Hebrew. Chalaqot is 'smoothnesses', slick, polished, slippery words (compare the 'smooth things' of Isa 30:10), and the parallel 'great things' is not 'proud things' but speech that swells, large promises and large claims, from a mouth that thinks itself unanswerable. Note the physical image: lips and a tongue, the body parts, are the targets, so that the speakers are reduced to their instruments. The KJV numbers this as verse 3.

philological_notes.note: 'He will cut off', or in prayer 'may he cut off'. The verb that makes a covenant (karat berit) and that cuts a person off from his people; both senses sound under the curse on those who broke their word.
'Smoothnesses': plural abstract of the root for smooth, slippery. English 'flattery' fits one use, but the Hebrew names the surface of the speech, not only its motive.
'Great things': words that grow large. Radak takes it as 'lofty' speech; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'important, precious', words used to deceive; Malbim hears matters of faith.

verses.translation_literal: Who have said, To our tongue we will make strong; our lips are with us; who is master to us?
verses.translation_dramatic: These are the ones who say: With our tongues we will win. Our lips are our own. Who is master over us?
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the boast of the men the previous verse condemns, quoted aloud, and the actor should let them hear themselves. 'Our lips are with us' is a claim of ownership: a man's speech is his property, answerable to no one. The closing question, 'who is lord over us?', is not idle: adon is the word for master, for the king and for the lord of a household, and in a world of oaths and witnesses speech was the thing the gods and the king were supposed to hold men to. These speakers declare themselves free of that, the sin the psalm answers in verse 7 with the words of the one true Lord.

The KJV 'with our tongue will we prevail' reads the lamed as 'with'; the Hebrew has 'to our tongue', and the readers disagree. Rashi takes it as 'by our tongue we will prevail'. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as 'because of / for the sake of our tongue', and Radak cites Gen 20:13 ('say of me, he is my brother') as parallel; Meiri takes the first lamed as extra, as in 'they killed Abner' (2 Sam 3:30), where the lamed marks the object. 'Our lips are our own' is the KJV's smooth English; the Hebrew says only 'with us', which can mean 'on our side', and the sense of ownership comes from that. Nagbir, from the root for strength, also makes 'gibbor', the warrior: they will be heroes by talk, not by sword.

philological_notes.note: 'To our tongue'. Rashi reads 'by our tongue'; Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'because of / for the sake of our tongue', Radak citing Gen 20:13; Meiri reads the first lamed as extra, citing 2 Sam 3:30. The literal layer keeps the lamed.
Hiphil, 'we will make strong' or 'we will prevail'; the root of gibbor, warrior. The boast is that talk will do what force does.
Master, lord, the one with rightful authority over another; also a title of God. Its use here with 'who' denies any such authority.

verses.translation_literal: From the devastation of the afflicted, from the groaning of the needy, now I will arise, says YHWH; I will set [him] in the safety [for which] he pants.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'Because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan, now I will rise,' says the LORD. 'I will set him in the safety he is gasping for.'
verses.directors_commentary: The whole psalm turns on this verse, and on one word: 'now'. After the speaker's long complaint, God himself speaks, and the only time he says 'I' in the psalm he says 'I will arise', the verb of a judge standing up from his seat or a warrior rising to act. The reason is not the speaker's cry but the groan of the poor: 'devastation' (shod) is violent plunder, 'groaning' (anaqah) is the sound of a prisoner. The KJV 'oppression' and 'sighing' are too mild; shod is robbery with force and anaqah is a groan. Then the difficult last clause, yafiach lo. The KJV 'from him that puffeth at him' reads a scornful blower; the ASV 'the safety he panteth for' reads a hungry gasper. The Hebrew breathes both ways, so play the line with breath: God sets the one who pants for rescue in the very breath of safety. Rashi reads 'speaks' (God will speak of them in safety); Radak reads 'a snare', from Proverbs 29:8, so the sense becomes 'safe from the trap laid for him'.

philological_notes.note: 'He breathes, pants, puffs, speaks'. The meaning is disputed: 'pants' (for rescue), 'puffs at' (scorns), 'speaks' (as in Prov 6:19, Hab 2:3) or 'sets a snare' (Prov 29:8). The verse can carry more than one.
Violent ruin, plunder, devastation; the verb is the one used for raiders. Rashi ties it to David and the priests of Nob (1 Sam 22).
The needy, the beggar, those who wish for something they lack; paired with 'ani, the afflicted, as in the Psalms' standard pair for the poor.

verses.translation_literal: The sayings of YHWH are sayings pure, silver refined in a crucible of the earth, purified sevenfold.
verses.translation_dramatic: The words of the LORD are clean words: silver refined in a furnace in the earth, and poured out again and again, seven times pure.
verses.directors_commentary: After the slick talk of men, the word of God. The contrast is built into the sounds: the same word 'amarot, 'sayings', twice, then 'pure'. Where the boasters' lips are smooth and shining, God's speech is silver that has been through fire and had its slag skimmed off. The picture is a smelter's: crude ore is heated, the silver sinks to the bottom or is poured off, the dross is removed, and the process repeats. 'Sevenfold' is not arithmetic; it is the number of completeness, and Radak and Ibn Ezra both say simply 'many times'. The hard word is ba'alil: it occurs only here, and the KJV 'furnace of earth' is a guess. Rashi lists readings: 'in the open', 'a vessel', 'a lord of the earth' (Ibn Ezra and Radak). Keep 'crucible' and do not let an actor explain it. The KJV 'tried' is archaic for 'assayed'; 'pure' is exactly right. Contrast with the previous verse: the lips promise nothing that holds, but this God said 'I will arise' and the claim is that it holds.

philological_notes.note: A unique word. 'In a crucible' (the lexical guess), 'in the open' (Rashi, after the Mishnah, Rosh Hashanah 1:5), 'in the best of' or 'a lord of' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, from ba'al). The meaning is not settled.
A dual form, 'sevenfold, seven times over'. Radak: seven stands for 'many', as in Lev 26:21 and Prov 24:16.

verses.translation_literal: You, YHWH, will keep them; you will guard him from the generation this, for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: You, LORD, will keep them. You will watch over each one, and keep him from this generation, for ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the silver, the plain trust: you, and only you. The pronoun comes first and carries the weight. The verse turns on a small shift the English versions hide: 'you will keep them' (tishmerem) is plural, but 'you will guard him' (titzerenu) is singular. Radak reads the singular as 'each and every poor person', wherever he stands among his oppressors; Meiri and Metzudat David say the same. The KJV and the ASV level the singular into 'them', which hides the shift from the many to the one; the YLT reads 'us', which makes the psalmist one of the poor. The Hebrew leaves the many and the one side by side, and the actor should let the voice come down from the crowd to a single person.

Two verbs for watching: shamar, to keep as a shepherd or a guard keeps, and natsar, to guard as a city is watched, to hold something precious. Nothing of 'this generation' is softened in the English; it is the psalmist's own age, and it is a stranger thing than it sounds. Radak says it means 'from this generation, which is wicked', and le'olam, 'for ever', he reads as 'in every generation': the guarding does not stop when this age does. Ibn Ezra reads the first verb as perhaps about the words of verse 7 rather than the poor, which would have God guarding the speech itself, and Malbim goes further, that he guards the words from forgers. The speaker should not decide; the object stays open for a breath. The KJV numbers this as verse 7.

philological_notes.note: 'You will guard him': singular suffix after plural 'them'. Radak: each and every poor person in the place where oppressors are. KJV and ASV read 'them'; YLT 'us'.
'This generation'. Zu is a poetic form of the demonstrative, here before the noun without matching article. Radak: this generation of the wicked; le'olam, 'in every generation'.

verses.translation_literal: All around, wicked ones walk about, as vileness is exalted by the sons of Adam.
verses.translation_dramatic: And still they prowl on every side, the wicked, strutting, while all that is vile is lifted high among the children of men.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends with no triumph, but with a picture of a street. The wicked go about 'all around', the poor man surrounded, and the verb is the reflexive-intensive yithallekhun: they stroll, they parade, with the confidence of men who fear nothing. Rashi reads it as men setting snares, Radak as the wicked circling the righteous to harm them.

The last line is hard, and the old commentators split. The Hebrew has an abstract noun, zulut, 'vileness, worthlessness', not 'the vilest men' as the KJV makes it: the KJV turns a quality into a class of persons, and in doing so loses the horror, that it is the thing itself, contempt and baseness, that is raised up. Meiri reads it as 'base things are admired': in this evil generation, disgrace and shame are held high and precious by people, who praise evil and hold to it. Radak reads it differently: when the wicked rise, it is disgrace and lowliness for humankind, as in 'when the wicked rule, the people groan' (Prov 29:2). Rashi gives the personal reading: when a man who is despised in men's eyes is exalted, as David was taken from behind the flock to be king, and their envy circles him. He also records Menahem's reading of the rare word rum as re'em, the wild ox, with zulut as 'glutton': the beast devouring men. Ibn Ezra hears zulut as kalon, 'disgrace'. The KJV numbers this as verse 8.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael with the older ending -un: 'they walk about', go back and forth, parade. The form shows habit and display.

'As vileness is exalted' (rum, 'height', zulut, 'vileness'). Meiri: base things are admired. Radak: when the wicked rise, it is disgrace for humankind (Prov 29:2). Rashi gives also Menahem: 'like the re'em, the glutton', devouring men.
